title: Drawn by the Father; flesh as bread; hard saying (John 6:37–62)
english: revelation. And "I will not cast out" (John 6:37) means this: I will not destroy, but will save and arrange for much care to be enjoyed.

Faith in me, he says, is no chance thing, but needs a tilt from above so one may know what is beyond mind, even if our own zeal is also sought. As a physician the Father brings weak humans to Christ, and by economy as man he assigns what befits God to the Father, since as God Christ is able to bring them to himself.
Therefore Jesus is not a bare man, but God incarnate, not deified after the resurrection; for the descent precedes the ascent.
I did not come having a will of my own apart from the Father; for all that is mine is the Father's and the Father's is mine, and I came to do nothing except what the Father also wills.

All humans rise, but only the faithful are counted worthy of the goods. The Son gives life to the faithful by putting the Spirit's life-giving power into humans corruptible by nature and remaking them wholly into immortality.
Because of his mother according to the flesh they thought it impossible that he had come down from heaven, or looking at what appeared and not considering his invisible nature they took offense.
If the Father draws and God raises, great is the dignity of the faithful. He does this as God by nature.

The Father draws those good by choice and leaves the wicked. The saying does not abolish what is in our power of free will, but shows that we need help; for one is drawn not unwillingly, but enjoying much alliance. The mystery concerning Christ is a good taught by God.

Even if the Father drew through the prophets' teaching, the difference is great: the first were taught through the prophets, but the faithful through the Son or the Holy Spirit. "All shall be taught by God" (John 6:45) stands for the greater number, or that God teaches all who are willing.
Hearing is common; learning belongs only to those who give themselves to grace.
The only Invisible appears in nature only to the Invisible. Only the Son sees the Father as existing outside all things and alone being from the Father's essence.
As giving eternal life to the faithful, or as sustaining our life both now and to come. For even if one tastes death, one does not remain so because of the hope of the resurrection.
He calls his own flesh bread because it is eaten in the mysteries.
As if the matter were contrary to nature they disbelieve; as soulish they do not understand the Lord's spiritual body. He does not speak of eating flesh, but of sharing in the mysteries.
You will be without share in eternal life who have not received through participation in the mysteries Jesus who is life by nature.
He says these things showing that the flesh was not of a bare man, but of the Son filled with all the Godhead as one of the Trinity.
Just as sensible foods mixed into us constitute the body, so also mystical participation makes a kind of natural joining of the believer with Christ by mixing.
The Son is life by nature, not having received living from another; for that is called a living being. So neither is the name living being assigned to God, nor the name life to the creation.
The one who believes that the bread is given from heaven also believes that he gives eternal life. Therefore those who ate the manna did not eat the bread from heaven, from which they died.
Why did he say these things in a synagogue? To teach the crowd the doctrines and that he was not opposed to God.
The evangelist said "the word is hard" (John 6:60) because they heard the Lord's words too humanly. Not understanding what was said, they could not bear even to ask and learn.
The incarnate God himself is the Son of Man. The body itself is not called Son of Man, as Marcellus wrongly teaches when he says he came down from heaven. He teaches that he was God

title: Spirit and flesh; Judas; Tabernacles counsel (John 6:62–7:27)
english: and was seen in flesh and that his flesh is life-giving.
That is: they are spiritual. They have no natural sequence, but are outside such necessity. Here he calls spirit the flesh filled with the Spirit's life-giving energy; for the flesh remains flesh.
Even if as God he knew they were going to disbelieve, still he speaks what benefits the common good.
"Many of his disciples" (John 6:66) does not mean the Twelve.

Knowing what would be, Jesus as God does the good and grants things worthy of wonder, yet he does not overturn our free will; for he does his own part, and it is in us to keep it. Hence one must not blame God for the benefits he gives, but those who willingly lost the gifts, as Adam, Eve, Judas, and all such. Even if I chose you, virtue and vice in humans are free. He calls devil the one clinging to the devil, made like him, and doing what pleases him.

As amazed the evangelist said "one of the Twelve" (John 6:71), that the devil wars so far as to be able to snatch one of the Twelve who raised dead and drove out demons and enjoyed the Lord's life-giving and spiritual teaching.
He shows the things of humanity by fleeing the Jews and convicting Marcion and Paul who said that God's Son did not truly become man.
His brothers seemed to blame him as cowardly and as doing signs in secret, wanting him as glory-loving to be in the open.
Here "world" means humans who mind the things of the world.
You do what you want without looking around; I do not, because I arrange each thing toward what is useful. I wait for the passion, that rising I may make my power plain to all.

It was not the same to stay at the feast's start while the Jews boiled with anger; so later, when the feast was about to end, he goes up, having done nothing contrary to what he said; for he did not go up to keep festival, but to counsel. Therefore he also went up secretly, not with the cheer festival-goers use. And in the old covenant, having said to Moses "I will not go up with you," later when Moses pleaded he promised to go with them.
From the difficulty they ought to have known that he is God.

Because of extreme likeness he calls his teaching the Father's, or because he himself is the Father's "wisdom" through which the Father speaks all things, or also as man by economy he assigns the teaching to the Father because of the Jews' unbelief. He says he was sent because of the flesh, or as Word from mind—that is, from the Father—or as "radiance" from the sun (Hebrews 1:3).
That is: privately and separately; for I would not speak otherwise than according to the Father's will.

What concerns himself he is silent about by economy because of the Jews' readiness to take offense and for blamelessness, and he proclaims the Father's glory. He weaves this argument so they may know he does not seek glory.

Being Lord of Moses and of the law, because of the Jews' weakness he somehow alienates himself from the law by calling it Moses'; for they could not hear that he was God by nature, nor the deep mystery of the economy.

Why are you troubled? For healing the paralytic did not loose the Sabbath; not healing did. When, he says, a person receives a sign that causes pain, no one is angry that the law is loosed; yet here, when a whole person has been healed, you are vexed as if lawlessness occurred.
If you do not blame those who circumcise or sacrifice or fight on the Sabbath, do not blame me either; for this is nothing other than respect of persons.
The crowd convicts the Jews who want to kill him and deny it—lying—while Christ speaks truth about himself.
You say well that when the Christ comes no one knows where he is from; for the true God from whom I am

title: Unknown origin; living water; light of the world (John 7:27–8:16)
english: has been unknown to you, he says, and it is no wonder if you do not know me, that I am the Christ, since you do not know the one from whom I am.

Those were saying about the Jerusalemites, "Have they not known that this is the Christ?" while they themselves held the opposite and said, "We know this man, that he is from earth and is 'son of the carpenter,' but as for the Christ, we do not know him."

He is visible to me alone, since I am God by nature and not of created nature, who know the Father only by thoughts as they can. But his Son contemplates the whole Begetter in himself and paints the Begetter's essence in his own nature, and so knows him as cannot be said; for the things concerning God are inexpressible.
From this we learn that he suffered willingly and was not seized by Jewish greed. By hour he means the timely outcome of the affairs.

By what they murmured they appear accepting Christ and wanting to split from the leaders. Sensing this, the leaders sent to seize him for this alone—that he was believed to be the Christ—so that they might destroy him.
When all were running together and about to go home, then he teaches, that they may have his words as provision for the way.
I drag no one by force, but the one who has much eagerness. He spoke thus to teach that those who run to faith ought to have the thirsting ones' desire, who when they drink find rest.
Since the law calls the seventh a "holy convocation," following old custom the evangelist also called it great.

The faithful will receive as faith's repayment abundant goods, and will have such a gift from the Holy Spirit that they not only rejoice themselves but also share the Spirit's grace with others, so that those too no longer thirst for knowledge of the truth.
He does not refer the saying to the hypostasis, but to the Spirit's energy, which came after Christ's resurrection.
They said well that the Christ must be from David's seed and from Bethlehem. They err because of Nazareth, where he was raised, though he was born in Bethlehem from the virgin of David.
He shows that he is the one of whom it was proclaimed beforehand, "I have set you as a light for the nations" (Isaiah 49:6), and not one of the prophets but Lord.

He called himself the light, not that the light is in me, lest someone cut the one Christ into a duality of sons; for there is one Christ Son both before flesh and after flesh, and one and only true Son from God and Father, and when he became man human nature is not set in a part; for the body is his own, and to cut Christ after the incarnation into two sons or two natures (for it is the same) is blasphemous.

If they had known that he was God's Son and came down from heaven, they would not have taken offense because of the visible body. "I am God," he says, "and I witness to myself worthily; but you do not know me for this reason, because you want to understand nothing except what appears." He did not say "I am God," but "where I come from," mixing lowly with high. "You do not know where I come from and where I go"; for they were willfully wicked and pretended not to know.
Looking at my appearing body you judge my affairs wrongly.
For I did not come for these things, since it is not a time of judgment; if I wanted to judge, you are among the condemned. "I did not come" now "to judge the world" but to save (John 12:47).

He says this toward the hearers' suspicion—that is, my judgment is the Father's, and I do not judge otherwise than the Father, nor the Father otherwise than the Son. He did not say this as weak about judging, but that with the Son the Father is going to judge those who disbelieve the one sent from him.
